title.sourceEnglish: Rainwater Tanks and Roof Catchment: Collecting and Protecting Water
title.xitsongaDraft: Mathanki ya mati ya mpfula ni Roof Catchment: Ku hlengeleta ni ku sirhelela mati

body.sourceEnglish:
Your roof can collect rainwater. The amount depends on roof area, rainfall and losses.

Check whether the roof material is suitable for rainwater collection before connecting a tank.

Use the roof area seen from above and local rainfall records. Then allow for water that misses the gutter, is diverted or overflows a full tank.

An annual total does not tell you how much water will be available during a dry spell. Compare supply with the uses you plan.

Roof runoff can carry dust, droppings and other contamination. A first-flush diverter keeps some of the first runoff out of the tank.

The required diversion depends on the roof and system. Use the supplier's sizing and maintenance instructions; there is no single volume for every roof.

A diverter does not make the remaining water safe to drink.

Tank size depends on water demand, rain, roof area and the length of dry periods.

List the intended uses and estimate their demand from your own records. Compare that with supply through the seasons.

Plan what you will do when stored water runs low. A province name alone cannot tell you the tank size you need.

Keep the tank covered, screen openings against insects, and maintain the roof, gutters and diverter. Keep rainwater separate from drinking-water pipes.

Water that looks clear may still contain germs or chemicals. Ask the local health authority about testing and treatment suited to the intended use.

A basic filter alone is not a drinking-water guarantee. Water used on food crops also needs a safety assessment.
body.xitsongaDraft:
Lwangu ra wena ri nga hlengeleta mati ya mpfula. Ntsengo wu titshege hi vukulu bya lwangu, mpfula na ku lahleka ka mati.

Kamba loko switirhisiwa swa lwangu swi faneleka ku hlengeleta mati ya mpfula u nga si hlanganisa thanki.

Tirhisa vukulu bya lwangu loko ri langutiwa hi le henhla na tirhekhodo ta mpfula ya le kusuhi. Kutani u tlhela u hlayela mati lama nga fikiki eka gutter, lama hambukisiwaka kumbe lama khulukaka ma huma eka thanki leyi teleke.

Ntsengo wa lembe hinkwaro a wu ku byeli leswaku ku ta kumeka mati yo tala ku fikela kwihi hi nkarhi wo oma. Pimanisa mati lama kumekaka na ku tirhisiwa ka mati loku u ku pulaneke.

Runoff ya lwangu yi nga rhwala ntshuri, droppings na contamination yin’wana. First-flush diverter yi hambukisa mati man’wana ya runoff yo sungula leswaku ma nga ngheni etankini.

Mati lama faneleke ku hambukisiwa ya titshege hi lwangu na system. Tirhisa swiletelo swa muphakeri swa sizing na maintenance; a ku na volume yin’we ya lwangu rin’wana na rin’wana.

Diverter a yi endli leswaku mati lawa ma saleke ma hlayiseka ku nwa.

Sayizi ya thanki yi titshege hi xilaveko xa mati, mpfula, vukulu bya lwangu na vulehi bya minkarhi yo oma.

Tsala ku tirhisiwa ka mati loku kunguhatiweke kutani u anganyela ntsengo wa mati lama lavekaka eka ku tirhisiwa koloko hi ku tirhisa tirhekhodo ta wena. Pimanisa ntsengo wolowo na mati lama kumekaka hi tinguva.

Kunguhatela leswi u nga ta swi endla loko mati lama hlayisiweke ma sungula ku va matsongo. Vito ra xifundzankulu ntsena a ri ku byeli vukulu bya thanki leyi u yi lavaka.

Hlayisa thanki yi funengetiwile. Funengeta timbobo hi screen leswaku switsotswana swi nga ngheni, naswona hlayisa lwangu, gutters na diverter. Hlayisa mati ya mpfula ma hambanile ni tiphayiphi ta mati yo nwa.

Mati lama vonakaka ma basile ma nga ha va na germs kumbe chemicals. Vutisa health authority ya laha kaya hi testing na treatment leswi fambisanaka ni ku tirhisiwa ka mati loku kunguhatiweke.

Basic filter ntsena a yi tiyisisi leswaku mati ma hlayisekile ku nwa. Mati lawa ya tirhisiwaka eka swirimiwa swa swakudya na wona ya lava nkambelo wa vuhlayiseki.

title.sourceEnglish: Greywater: Check Before Reuse
title.xitsongaDraft: Greywater: Kambela u nga si ma tirhisa nakambe

body.sourceEnglish:
Used household water can contain germs, salts, cleaning products and other substances. Guidance does not define every source in the same way. South African guidance differs on kitchen water and laundry water.

Do not include toilet water, water from nappies, washing a sick person or washing animals in a reuse plan. Do not reuse water containing harmful chemicals.

Before any reuse, ask the municipality and a qualified local sanitation adviser to check the exact source, the household's water and sanitation services, the intended use and the site. If this advice is unavailable or unclear, do not reuse the water.

A generic picture is not a farm design. Soil and mulch do not disinfect wastewater. Keep it away from drinking-water plumbing and prevent contact with people or animals. Do not spray it, let it pool, or allow it to run off the property into a street, drain or watercourse.

If a reuse system is already operating and the water smells bad, pools or harms plants, stop using it and seek qualified local advice.
body.xitsongaDraft:
Mati lama tirhisiweke ekaya ma nga va na germs, salts, cleaning products ni swilo swin’wana. Swiletelo a swi hlamuseli swihlovo hinkwato hi ndlela yin’we. Swiletelo swa Afrika-Dzonga swi hambana hi mati ya le khixini ni mati yo hlantswa swiambalo.

U nga katsi mati ya xihambukelo, mati yo huma eka nappies, mati yo hlantswa munhu loyi a vabyaka kumbe mati yo hlantswa swiharhi eka pulani yo tirhisa mati nakambe. U nga tirhisi nakambe mati lama nga na chemicals leti nga ni khombo.

Before any reuse, kombela masipala na mutsundzuxi wa sanitation wa laha kaya loyi a nga qualified ku kambela xihlovo xa mati lexi kongomeke, vukorhokeri bya mati na sanitation bya ndyangu, ku tirhisiwa loku kunguhatiweke na ndhawu. Loko ndzayo leyi yi nga kumeki kumbe yi nga ri erivaleni, u nga ma tirhisi nakambe.

Xifaniso xo angarhela a hi pulani ya purasi. Misava ni mulch a swi disinfect wastewater. Hlayisa wastewater yi ri ekule ni plumbing ya mati yo nwa naswona u sivela leswaku yi khumba vanhu kumbe swiharhi. U nga ma fafazeli, u nga ma tshiki ma pool, naswona u nga ma pfumeleli ku khuluka ma huma eka property ma nghena exitarateni, eka drain kumbe eka watercourse.

Loko system yo tirhisa mati nakambe yi se ri karhi yi tirha naswona mati ma nunha, ma pool kumbe ma onha swimilana, tshika ku ma tirhisa kutani u lava ndzayo ya mutsundzuxi wa laha kaya loyi a nga qualified.

english.heading: Soil Health & Composting
body: Soil is more than the ground under your feet.
It is a living place that feeds crops, holds water, and carries your harvest.
In this module, learn to read soil, make safe compost, protect bare ground, and use cover crops and worm farms.

heading.text: Bophelo ba mobu le ho etsa compost

body.text: Mobu ha se feela sebaka seo u hatang ho sona.
Ke sebaka se phelang se fepang dijalo, se tshwarang metsi, mme se jereng kotulo ya hao.

english.heading: Why This Matters
body: Soil condition affects roots, water and the harvest.
Repeated bare ground, compaction and loss of organic matter can damage it. Colour alone does not tell the whole story.
Observe your soil, then choose ways to protect and improve it.

heading.text: Lebaka leo sena se leng bohlokoa

body: Look for several clues about soil condition.
Use a jar to explore soil texture, while recognising its limits.
Care for a compost heap, protect bare ground, and distinguish worm castings from liquid drainage.

english.heading: Soil Is Alive
body: Soil contains many kinds of living organisms. Bacteria and fungi help break down organic matter and cycle nutrients.
Some fungi help roots take up nutrients. Worm channels can help water and air enter soil.
Look at roots, soil structure and water movement as well as visible soil life.

english.heading: Watch: Read Your Soil
body: Look closely at these two soil examples.
First, look at soil structure. In the field, feel how a moist piece breaks apart.
Look at the roots and the spaces around them.
Look at the surface cover. Loose mulch covers one example.
Use several clues together. Colour alone cannot tell you soil health. Check moisture, plant growth and how water enters the ground.

english.heading: Explore Soil Texture with a Jar
body: Put soil and water in a clear jar, with a little suitable dispersing detergent. Close and shake it, then leave it undisturbed.
Sand settles first. Silt settles next, while clay can remain suspended much longer.
This is a rough learning exercise. Clumps and unsettled clay can mislead you; use a soil laboratory when accurate texture is needed.

body.text: Kenya mobu le metsi ka jar e bonaletsang, o kenye hanyenyane ya suitable dispersing detergent. E kwale mme o e sisinye, ebe o e siya e sa sisinyehe.

body.text: Ena ke boikwetliso ba ho ithuta ba kakanyo feela. Dikgobokano tsa mobu (clumps) le clay e so duleng fatshe di ka o kgelosa; sebedisa soil laboratory ha o hloka soil texture e nepahetseng.

english.heading: Read the Jar Carefully
body: A thick sand layer beneath cloudy water does not yet tell you the final proportions. Some fine particles may still be suspended.
Compare the settled layers and feel the soil in the field.
Record what you see and what remains uncertain. Do not prescribe watering or soil treatments from one jar alone.

english.heading: Investigate Before You Treat
body: Compaction, poor drainage and loss of organic matter can limit roots and soil life.
Pale colour or few worms do not prove that chemicals killed the soil. Worm activity also changes with moisture and season.
Look for patterns across the field. Check management history, drainage and plant growth before choosing a remedy.

english.heading: Compost Feeds the Soil
body: Compost is organic matter broken down under managed conditions.
Finished compost can improve soil structure and contribute nutrients.
Time to readiness varies with materials, moisture, air and temperature. A province name or a fixed number of weeks is not a readiness test.

body: Build the heap with dry browns and fresh greens.
Keep the layers moist, not wet, so air and decomposers can work.

body: Mix dry browns with fresh greens. Avoid thick, wet layers that keep air out.
If the heap becomes slimy or smells strongly of ammonia, add dry browns and turn it.

english.heading: Heat Alone Is Not a Safety Check
body: A hot centre does not prove that every part of a heap has been treated. Time, temperature and management all matter.
Keep meat, dairy, diseased plants, pet waste and contaminated materials out of this simple household system.
Do not assume home composting destroys every weed seed or disease organism. Use a recognised process where sanitation is required.

english.heading: Keep Seed Pods and Contaminants Out
body: Keep wattle seed pods out of the compost heap. An ordinary heap may not make every seed non-viable.
Use only clean, untreated materials. Bark breaks down slowly; its name alone is not proof that it is free of contamination.
Check the heap and turn when it needs more air or mixing. Keep it moist rather than waterlogged.

english.heading: Watch: Bare Soil and Mulch
body: Compare bare soil with mulched soil.
When rain hits mulch instead of bare soil, much of the raindrop energy is dissipated. This diagram shows that surface-impact idea only; it does not predict how water will move at a particular site.

body.text: Bapisa mobu o sa kwahelwang le mobu o kwahetsweng ka mulch.

Ha pula e otla mulch ho e-na le mobu o sa kwahelwang, bongata ba matla a marothodi a pula bo a nyamela. Setshwantsho sena se bontsha feela mohopolo ona wa tshusumetso ya bokahodimo; ha se bolele esale pele hore metsi a tla tsamaya jwang sebakeng se itseng.

english.heading: Mulch Protects the Ground
body: Cover bare soil with suitable clean mulch, such as straw, dry grass or wood chips.
Mulch can reduce evaporation, soften the impact of rain and suppress weeds.
Keep it clear of trunks and stems. Check moisture underneath and adjust the layer; more mulch is not always better.

body.text: Koahela mobu o pepesitsweng ka mulch e hlwekileng e loketseng, jwalo ka straw, jwang bo ommeng kapa wood chips.

body.text: Mulch e ka fokotsa ho fetoha mouwane ha metsi, ya fokotsa matla ao pula e otlang mobu ka wona, hape ya fokotsa mefoka.

english.heading: Cover Crops Between Seasons
body: Cover crops can protect ground between main crops. Choose for local weather, available water and the next planting.
The course examples include oats, lupins, sunn hemp and cowpea. Check local suitability before sowing.
Legumes need suitable bacteria and growing conditions to fix nitrogen. Nutrients in their residues become available as the material decomposes.

heading.text: Cover Crops Pakeng tsa Dihla
heading.provenance: Bounded deck-only machine draft (Soil/Water ordinary-prose completion, 4–5 October 2026): drafted, blind back-translated and semantically checked by separate AI agents; difficult technical English retained. Unreviewed; not fluent or local farming approval.

body.text: Cover crops di ka sireletsa mobu pakeng tsa dijalo tse ka sehloohong. Di kgethe ho latela boemo ba lehodimo ba sebakeng sa heno, metsi a fumanehang le ho lema ho latelang.

body.text: Mehlala ya thuto ena e kenyelletsa oats, lupins, sunn hemp le cowpea. Hlahloba hore di loketse sebaka sa heno pele o jala.

body.text: Legumes di hloka bacteria tse loketseng le maemo a kgolo a loketseng hore di kgone ho fix nitrogen. Dimatlafatsi tse masalleng a tsona di a fumaneha ha thepa eo e ntse e bola.

english.heading: Worm Castings and Liquid Drainage
body: Worm farms can turn suitable food scraps and bedding into castings. Check the bin rather than expecting a fixed harvest date.
Liquid that drains naturally from a worm bin is called leachate. It is not the same as a prepared worm-casting tea.
Leachate can contain harmful organisms or substances. Do not use it on edible plants or assume that dilution makes it safe.

body.text: Mokedikedi o itshollang ka tlhaho ho tswa ho worm bin o bitswa leachate. Ha o tshwane le worm-casting tea e lokisitsweng.

english.heading: Protect Soil All Year
body: A Highveld field left bare after the maize harvest faces two main risks.
Winter wind can carry away dry topsoil.
The first heavy spring storm can strike bare ground and damage its surface and structure. If water runs over the field, it can carry loosened soil away.
Cover crops, mulch, and organic matter can help hold soil in place and help it stay alive.

body.text: Tshimo ya Highveld e siilweng e sa kwahelwa ka mora kotulo ya poone (maize) e tobana le dikotsi tse pedi tse ka sehloohong.

Sefefo sa pele se matla sa selemo se ka otla mobu o sa kwahelwang, sa senya bokahodimo le sebopeho sa wona. Ha metsi a phalla a feta tshimong, a ka nka mobu o hlephileng a o tlosa.
Dijalo tse sireletsang mobu (cover crops), mulch le organic matter di ka thusa ho tshwara mobu sebakeng sa wona le ho o thusa hore o dule o phela.

body: Inspect soil in a working area. Record colour, structure, roots, moisture and any worm channels.
Compare another spot and note recent weather and management.
Try the jar exercise. Write what it suggests, what is uncertain, and whether a laboratory test or local adviser could help.

english.heading: Field Action
body: Start one soil-building action from this module.
Cover bare ground with mulch, begin a balanced compost heap, sow a suitable cover crop, or prepare a worm farm.
If your compost smells of ammonia and feels slimy, add dry carbon such as straw and turn it.
Build soil life step by step.

english.heading: Soil Health & Composting
body: Soil is more than the ground under your feet.
It is a living place that feeds crops, holds water, and carries your harvest.
In this module, learn to read soil, make safe compost, protect bare ground, and use cover crops and worm farms.

english.heading: Why This Matters
body: Soil condition affects roots, water and the harvest.
Repeated bare ground, compaction and loss of organic matter can damage it. Colour alone does not tell the whole story.
Observe your soil, then choose ways to protect and improve it.

body: Look for several clues about soil condition.
Use a jar to explore soil texture, while recognising its limits.
Care for a compost heap, protect bare ground, and distinguish worm castings from liquid drainage.

english.heading: Soil Is Alive
body: Soil contains many kinds of living organisms. Bacteria and fungi help break down organic matter and cycle nutrients.
Some fungi help roots take up nutrients. Worm channels can help water and air enter soil.
Look at roots, soil structure and water movement as well as visible soil life.

english.heading: Watch: Read Your Soil
body: Look closely at these two soil examples.
First, look at soil structure. In the field, feel how a moist piece breaks apart.
Look at the roots and the spaces around them.
Look at the surface cover. Loose mulch covers one example.
Use several clues together. Colour alone cannot tell you soil health. Check moisture, plant growth and how water enters the ground.

english.heading: Explore Soil Texture with a Jar
body: Put soil and water in a clear jar, with a little suitable dispersing detergent. Close and shake it, then leave it undisturbed.
Sand settles first. Silt settles next, while clay can remain suspended much longer.
This is a rough learning exercise. Clumps and unsettled clay can mislead you; use a soil laboratory when accurate texture is needed.

english.heading: Read the Jar Carefully
body: A thick sand layer beneath cloudy water does not yet tell you the final proportions. Some fine particles may still be suspended.
Compare the settled layers and feel the soil in the field.
Record what you see and what remains uncertain. Do not prescribe watering or soil treatments from one jar alone.

english.heading: Investigate Before You Treat
body: Compaction, poor drainage and loss of organic matter can limit roots and soil life.
Pale colour or few worms do not prove that chemicals killed the soil. Worm activity also changes with moisture and season.
Look for patterns across the field. Check management history, drainage and plant growth before choosing a remedy.

english.heading: Compost Feeds the Soil
body: Compost is organic matter broken down under managed conditions.
Finished compost can improve soil structure and contribute nutrients.
Time to readiness varies with materials, moisture, air and temperature. A province name or a fixed number of weeks is not a readiness test.

body: Build the heap with dry browns and fresh greens.
Keep the layers moist, not wet, so air and decomposers can work.

body: Mix dry browns with fresh greens. Avoid thick, wet layers that keep air out.
If the heap becomes slimy or smells strongly of ammonia, add dry browns and turn it.
Check moisture and air as the heap changes; one recipe does not suit every mix of materials.

english.heading: Heat Alone Is Not a Safety Check
body: A hot centre does not prove that every part of a heap has been treated. Time, temperature and management all matter.
Keep meat, dairy, diseased plants, pet waste and contaminated materials out of this simple household system.
Do not assume home composting destroys every weed seed or disease organism. Use a recognised process where sanitation is required.

english.heading: Keep Seed Pods and Contaminants Out
body: Keep wattle seed pods out of the compost heap. An ordinary heap may not make every seed non-viable.
Use only clean, untreated materials. Bark breaks down slowly; its name alone is not proof that it is free of contamination.
Check the heap and turn when it needs more air or mixing. Keep it moist rather than waterlogged.

english.heading: Watch: Bare Soil and Mulch
body: Compare bare soil with mulched soil.
When rain hits mulch instead of bare soil, much of the raindrop energy is dissipated. This diagram shows that surface-impact idea only; it does not predict how water will move at a particular site.

Musi mvula i tshi rwa mulch fhedzi hu si mavu a songo fukwaho, vhunzhi ha maanḓa a marothi a mvula vhu a fhungudzea. Tshifanyiso itshi tshi sumbedza fhedzi muhumbulo wa u rwa ha marothi a mvula nṱha ha mavu; a tshi ambi phanḓa uri maḓi a ḓo tshimbila hani fhethu huthihi hune ha khetheaho.

english.heading: Mulch Protects the Ground
body: Cover bare soil with suitable clean mulch, such as straw, dry grass or wood chips.
Mulch can reduce evaporation, soften the impact of rain and suppress weeds.
Keep it clear of trunks and stems. Check moisture underneath and adjust the layer; more mulch is not always better.

english.heading: Cover Crops Between Seasons
body: Cover crops can protect ground between main crops. Choose for local weather, available water and the next planting.
The course examples include oats, lupins, sunn hemp and cowpea. Check local suitability before sowing.
Legumes need suitable bacteria and growing conditions to fix nitrogen. Nutrients in their residues become available as the material decomposes.

english.heading: Worm Castings and Liquid Drainage
body: Worm farms can turn suitable food scraps and bedding into castings. Check the bin rather than expecting a fixed harvest date.
Liquid that drains naturally from a worm bin is called leachate. It is not the same as a prepared worm-casting tea.
Leachate can contain harmful organisms or substances. Do not use it on edible plants or assume that dilution makes it safe.

english.heading: Protect Soil All Year
body: A Highveld field left bare after the maize harvest faces two main risks.
Winter wind can carry away dry topsoil.
The first heavy spring storm can strike bare ground and damage its surface and structure. If water runs over the field, it can carry loosened soil away.
Cover crops, mulch, and organic matter can help hold soil in place and help it stay alive.

Compare another spot and note recent weather and management.
Try the jar exercise. Write what it suggests, what is uncertain, and whether a laboratory test or local adviser could help.

english.heading: Soil Health & Composting
body: Soil is more than the ground under your feet.
It is a living place that feeds crops, holds water, and carries your harvest.
In this module, learn to read soil, make safe compost, protect bare ground, and use cover crops and worm farms.

english.heading: Why This Matters
body: Soil condition affects roots, water and the harvest.
Repeated bare ground, compaction and loss of organic matter can damage it. Colour alone does not tell the whole story.
Observe your soil, then choose ways to protect and improve it.

body: Look for several clues about soil condition.
Use a jar to explore soil texture, while recognising its limits.
Care for a compost heap, protect bare ground, and distinguish worm castings from liquid drainage.

english.heading: Soil Is Alive
body: Soil contains many kinds of living organisms. Bacteria and fungi help break down organic matter and cycle nutrients.
Some fungi help roots take up nutrients. Worm channels can help water and air enter soil.
Look at roots, soil structure and water movement as well as visible soil life.

english.heading: Watch: Read Your Soil
body: Look closely at these two soil examples.
First, look at soil structure. In the field, feel how a moist piece breaks apart.
Look at the roots and the spaces around them.
Look at the surface cover. Loose mulch covers one example.
Use several clues together. Colour alone cannot tell you soil health. Check moisture, plant growth and how water enters the ground.

english.heading: Explore Soil Texture with a Jar
body: Put soil and water in a clear jar, with a little suitable dispersing detergent. Close and shake it, then leave it undisturbed.
Sand settles first. Silt settles next, while clay can remain suspended much longer.
This is a rough learning exercise. Clumps and unsettled clay can mislead you; use a soil laboratory when accurate texture is needed.

Compare the settled layers and feel the soil in the field.
Record what you see and what remains uncertain. Do not prescribe watering or soil treatments from one jar alone.

body: Compaction, poor drainage and loss of organic matter can limit roots and soil life.
Pale colour or few worms do not prove that chemicals killed the soil. Worm activity also changes with moisture and season.
Look for patterns across the field. Check management history, drainage and plant growth before choosing a remedy.

Finished compost can improve soil structure and contribute nutrients.

english.heading: Heat Alone Is Not a Safety Check
body: A hot centre does not prove that every part of a heap has been treated. Time, temperature and management all matter.
Keep meat, dairy, diseased plants, pet waste and contaminated materials out of this simple household system.
Do not assume home composting destroys every weed seed or disease organism. Use a recognised process where sanitation is required.

english.heading: Keep Seed Pods and Contaminants Out
body: Keep wattle seed pods out of the compost heap. An ordinary heap may not make every seed non-viable.
Use only clean, untreated materials. Bark breaks down slowly; its name alone is not proof that it is free of contamination.
Check the heap and turn when it needs more air or mixing. Keep it moist rather than waterlogged.

body: Compare bare soil with mulched soil.
When rain hits mulch instead of bare soil, much of the raindrop energy is dissipated. This diagram shows that surface-impact idea only; it does not predict how water will move at a particular site.

english.heading: Mulch Protects the Ground
body: Cover bare soil with suitable clean mulch, such as straw, dry grass or wood chips.
Mulch can reduce evaporation, soften the impact of rain and suppress weeds.
Keep it clear of trunks and stems. Check moisture underneath and adjust the layer; more mulch is not always better.

english.heading: Cover Crops Between Seasons
body: Cover crops can protect ground between main crops. Choose for local weather, available water and the next planting.
The course examples include oats, lupins, sunn hemp and cowpea. Check local suitability before sowing.
Legumes need suitable bacteria and growing conditions to fix nitrogen. Nutrients in their residues become available as the material decomposes.

english.heading: Worm Castings and Liquid Drainage
body: Worm farms can turn suitable food scraps and bedding into castings. Check the bin rather than expecting a fixed harvest date.
Liquid that drains naturally from a worm bin is called leachate. It is not the same as a prepared worm-casting tea.
Leachate can contain harmful organisms or substances. Do not use it on edible plants or assume that dilution makes it safe.

english.heading: Protect Soil All Year
body: A Highveld field left bare after the maize harvest faces two main risks.
Winter wind can carry away dry topsoil.
The first heavy spring storm can strike bare ground and damage its surface and structure. If water runs over the field, it can carry loosened soil away.
Cover crops, mulch, and organic matter can help hold soil in place and help it stay alive.

english.heading: Two Swale Designs
body: A level contour swale is one design for slowing runoff. Its trench follows a level contour so water can spread and soak into suitable soil.

Some swales are deliberately given a slight grade, with a designed safe outlet. Soil, slope, drainage and storm flow decide which approach is suitable. Ask a trained local adviser to assess the site before digging.

english.heading: Storms Need a Safe Overflow
body: Heavy rain can fill a swale faster than water soaks into the soil. Plan a safe overflow before digging.
The route must not erode the slope or send damaging water to a neighbour. A downstream swale or dam must be able to receive it safely.
Ask a trained local adviser to assess the soil, slope and storm flow. A picture is not a construction design.

english.heading: Check the Site Before Digging
body: Slope alone does not tell you whether a swale is suitable. Soil, drainage, unstable ground and the water arriving from upslope all matter.
Keep good ground cover. Get a local assessment before digging on steep, wet or unstable land. Grass barriers and terraces also need a design suited to the site.

english.heading: Store Rain for the Dry Season
body: A dam or pond can store runoff, but the amount available depends on local rain, the catchment, losses and how much water you use.
Rainfall seasons differ across South Africa. Use local records and plan for dry periods; a full dam is not guaranteed.
Before changing a watercourse or building storage works, check the required authorisation with the water authority.

english.heading: Design the Spillway Before the Wall
body: A dam needs a site investigation and a design by a suitably qualified person. Catchment runoff, soil, foundations, downstream risk and a safe spillway all matter.
Do not assume that annual rainfall tells you the size of a flood or the storage you will have.
An uncontrolled overflow can erode and breach the wall. Plan a safe route for excess water before construction.

body: Design the spillway before the wall — an overtopped wall can breach catastrophically.
Catchment runoff is one input. A suitably qualified person must assess the site, dam and spillway design before construction.

english.heading: Care for the Dam and Its Banks
body: Water can be lost through evaporation and seepage. Check the water level and look for leaks or erosion.
Keep the spillway clear and maintain the bank cover specified in the design. Do not plant trees on an earth dam wall.
Animals can damage banks and add manure to the water. Their presence does not make the water clean or safe.

english.heading: Your Roof Is a Harvesting Surface
body: Your roof can collect rainwater. The amount depends on roof area, rainfall and losses.
Check whether the roof material is suitable for rainwater collection before connecting a tank.
Use the roof area seen from above and local rainfall records. Then allow for water that misses the gutter, is diverted or overflows a full tank.
An annual total does not tell you how much water will be available during a dry spell. Compare supply with the uses you plan.

english.heading: Divert the Dirty First Flush
body: Roof runoff can carry dust, droppings and other contamination. A first-flush diverter keeps some of the first runoff out of the tank.
The required diversion depends on the roof and system. Use the supplier's sizing and maintenance instructions; there is no single volume for every roof.
A diverter does not make the remaining water safe to drink.

Plan what you will do when stored water runs low. A province name alone cannot tell you the tank size you need.

english.heading: Keep Stored Water Protected
body: Keep the tank covered, screen openings against insects, and maintain the roof, gutters and diverter. Keep rainwater separate from drinking-water pipes.
Water that looks clear may still contain germs or chemicals. Ask the local health authority about testing and treatment suited to the intended use.
A basic filter alone is not a drinking-water guarantee. Water used on food crops also needs a safety assessment.

english.heading: Used Water Varies by Source
body: Used household water can contain germs, salts, cleaning products and other substances. Guidance does not define every source in the same way.

South African guidance differs on kitchen water and laundry water. Do not include toilet water, water from nappies, washing a sick person or washing animals in a reuse plan. Do not reuse water containing harmful chemicals.

english.heading: Get Local Advice Before Any Reuse
body: Before any reuse, ask the municipality and a qualified local sanitation adviser to check the exact source, the household's water and sanitation services, the intended use and the site.
If this advice is unavailable or unclear, do not reuse the water. Soil and mulch do not disinfect wastewater.

english.heading: Prevent Contact and Pollution
body: Prevent contact with people or animals. Do not connect washwater to drinking-water plumbing, spray it, let it pool, or allow it to run off the property into a street, drain or watercourse.
If a reuse system is already operating and the water smells bad, pools or harms plants, stop using it and seek qualified local advice.

english.heading: Water Harvesting
body: Swales, berms, dams, rainwater tanks and greywater — slow, spread and sink every drop.

english.heading: Learning Outcomes
body: Explain how a level contour swale can slow and spread runoff for infiltration on a suitable site.
Explain why dams need a designed spillway and a site assessment.
Explain what a first-flush diverter does and why tank water still needs a safety check.
Keep greywater away from people, food and drinking-water pipes.

english.heading: Two Swale Designs
body: A level contour swale is one design for slowing runoff. Its trench follows a level contour so water can spread and soak into suitable soil.

Some swales are deliberately given a slight grade, with a designed safe outlet. Soil, slope, drainage and storm flow decide which approach is suitable. Ask a trained local adviser to assess the site before digging.

english.heading: The Downhill Berm
body: The excavated soil forms a berm on the downhill side. It is where trees may be planted when the site design is suitable.
Trees may draw on moisture stored in nearby soil after rain; the result varies by site.

english.heading: Storms Need a Safe Overflow
body: Heavy rain can fill a swale faster than water soaks into the soil. Plan a safe overflow before digging.
The route must not erode the slope or send damaging water to a neighbour. A downstream swale or dam must be able to receive it safely.
Ask a trained local adviser to assess the soil, slope and storm flow. A picture is not a construction design.

Water may go to another swale or a dam only when a site assessment shows that the route, outlet and receiver can take the flow without damage.

english.heading: Check the Site Before Digging
body: Slope alone does not tell you whether a swale is suitable. Soil, drainage, unstable ground and the water arriving from upslope all matter.
Keep good ground cover. Get a local assessment before digging on steep, wet or unstable land. Grass barriers and terraces also need a design suited to the site.

english.heading: Store Rain for the Dry Season
body: A dam or pond can store runoff, but the amount available depends on local rain, the catchment, losses and how much water you use.
Rainfall seasons differ across South Africa. Use local records and plan for dry periods; a full dam is not guaranteed.
Before changing a watercourse or building storage works, check the required authorisation with the water authority.

english.heading: Design the Spillway Before the Wall
body: A dam needs a site investigation and a design by a suitably qualified person. Catchment runoff, soil, foundations, downstream risk and a safe spillway all matter.
Do not assume that annual rainfall tells you the size of a flood or the storage you will have.
An uncontrolled overflow can erode and breach the wall. Plan a safe route for excess water before construction.

body: Design the spillway before the wall — an overtopped wall can breach catastrophically.

english.heading: Care for the Dam and Its Banks
body: Water can be lost through evaporation and seepage. Check the water level and look for leaks or erosion.
Keep the spillway clear and maintain the bank cover specified in the design. Do not plant trees on an earth dam wall.
Animals can damage banks and add manure to the water. Their presence does not make the water clean or safe.

english.heading: Your Roof Is a Harvesting Surface
body: Your roof can collect rainwater. The amount depends on roof area, rainfall and losses.
Check whether the roof material is suitable for rainwater collection before connecting a tank.
Use the roof area seen from above and local rainfall records. Then allow for water that misses the gutter, is diverted or overflows a full tank.
An annual total does not tell you how much water will be available during a dry spell. Compare supply with the uses you plan.

english.heading: Divert the Dirty First Flush
body: Roof runoff can carry dust, droppings and other contamination. A first-flush diverter keeps some of the first runoff out of the tank.
The required diversion depends on the roof and system. Use the supplier's sizing and maintenance instructions; there is no single volume for every roof.
A diverter does not make the remaining water safe to drink.

english.heading: Match Tank Size to Water Demand
body: Tank size depends on water demand, rain, roof area and the length of dry periods.
List the intended uses and estimate their demand from your own records. Compare that with supply through the seasons.
Plan what you will do when stored water runs low. A province name alone cannot tell you the tank size you need.

english.heading: Keep Stored Water Protected
body: Keep the tank covered, screen openings against insects, and maintain the roof, gutters and diverter. Keep rainwater separate from drinking-water pipes.
Water that looks clear may still contain germs or chemicals. Ask the local health authority about testing and treatment suited to the intended use.
A basic filter alone is not a drinking-water guarantee. Water used on food crops also needs a safety assessment.

english.heading: Used Water Varies by Source
body: Used household water can contain germs, salts, cleaning products and other substances. Guidance does not define every source in the same way.

South African guidance differs on kitchen water and laundry water. Do not include toilet water, water from nappies, washing a sick person or washing animals in a reuse plan. Do not reuse water containing harmful chemicals.

english.heading: Get Local Advice Before Any Reuse
body: Before any reuse, ask the municipality and a qualified local sanitation adviser to check the exact source, the household's water and sanitation services, the intended use and the site.
If this advice is unavailable or unclear, do not reuse the water. Soil and mulch do not disinfect wastewater.

english.heading: Prevent Contact and Pollution
body: Prevent contact with people or animals. Do not connect washwater to drinking-water plumbing, spray it, let it pool, or allow it to run off the property into a street, drain or watercourse.
If a reuse system is already operating and the water smells bad, pools or harms plants, stop using it and seek qualified local advice.

body: Explain how a level contour swale can slow and spread runoff for infiltration on a suitable site.

Keep greywater away from people, food and drinking-water pipes.

english.heading: Two Swale Designs
body: A level contour swale is one design for slowing runoff. Its trench follows a level contour so water can spread and soak into suitable soil.

Some swales are deliberately given a slight grade, with a designed safe outlet. Soil, slope, drainage and storm flow decide which approach is suitable. Ask a trained local adviser to assess the site before digging.

english.heading: Storms Need a Safe Overflow
body: Heavy rain can fill a swale faster than water soaks into the soil. Plan a safe overflow before digging.
The route must not erode the slope or send damaging water to a neighbour. A downstream swale or dam must be able to receive it safely.
Ask a trained local adviser to assess the soil, slope and storm flow. A picture is not a construction design.

english.heading: Assess the Overflow Before Digging
body: A swale needs a planned overflow route for heavy rain. Check it before digging.
Water may go to another swale or a dam only when a site assessment shows that the route, outlet and receiver can take the flow without damage.

english.heading: Check the Site Before Digging
body: Slope alone does not tell you whether a swale is suitable. Soil, drainage, unstable ground and the water arriving from upslope all matter.
Keep good ground cover. Get a local assessment before digging on steep, wet or unstable land. Grass barriers and terraces also need a design suited to the site.

english.heading: Store Rain for the Dry Season
body: A dam or pond can store runoff, but the amount available depends on local rain, the catchment, losses and how much water you use.
Rainfall seasons differ across South Africa. Use local records and plan for dry periods; a full dam is not guaranteed.
Before changing a watercourse or building storage works, check the required authorisation with the water authority.

english.heading: Design the Spillway Before the Wall
body: A dam needs a site investigation and a design by a suitably qualified person. Catchment runoff, soil, foundations, downstream risk and a safe spillway all matter.
Do not assume that annual rainfall tells you the size of a flood or the storage you will have.
An uncontrolled overflow can erode and breach the wall. Plan a safe route for excess water before construction.

english.heading: Care for the Dam and Its Banks
body: Water can be lost through evaporation and seepage. Check the water level and look for leaks or erosion.
Keep the spillway clear and maintain the bank cover specified in the design. Do not plant trees on an earth dam wall.
Animals can damage banks and add manure to the water. Their presence does not make the water clean or safe.

english.heading: Your Roof Is a Harvesting Surface
body: Your roof can collect rainwater. The amount depends on roof area, rainfall and losses.
Check whether the roof material is suitable for rainwater collection before connecting a tank.
Use the roof area seen from above and local rainfall records. Then allow for water that misses the gutter, is diverted or overflows a full tank.
An annual total does not tell you how much water will be available during a dry spell. Compare supply with the uses you plan.

english.heading: Divert the Dirty First Flush
body: Roof runoff can carry dust, droppings and other contamination. A first-flush diverter keeps some of the first runoff out of the tank.
The required diversion depends on the roof and system. Use the supplier's sizing and maintenance instructions; there is no single volume for every roof.
A diverter does not make the remaining water safe to drink.

Plan what you will do when stored water runs low. A province name alone cannot tell you the tank size you need.

english.heading: Keep Stored Water Protected
body: Keep the tank covered, screen openings against insects, and maintain the roof, gutters and diverter. Keep rainwater separate from drinking-water pipes.
Water that looks clear may still contain germs or chemicals. Ask the local health authority about testing and treatment suited to the intended use.
A basic filter alone is not a drinking-water guarantee. Water used on food crops also needs a safety assessment.

english.heading: Used Water Varies by Source
body: Used household water can contain germs, salts, cleaning products and other substances. Guidance does not define every source in the same way.

South African guidance differs on kitchen water and laundry water. Do not include toilet water, water from nappies, washing a sick person or washing animals in a reuse plan. Do not reuse water containing harmful chemicals.

english.heading: Get Local Advice Before Any Reuse
body: Before any reuse, ask the municipality and a qualified local sanitation adviser to check the exact source, the household's water and sanitation services, the intended use and the site.
If this advice is unavailable or unclear, do not reuse the water. Soil and mulch do not disinfect wastewater.

english.heading: Prevent Contact and Pollution
body: Prevent contact with people or animals. Do not connect washwater to drinking-water plumbing, spray it, let it pool, or allow it to run off the property into a street, drain or watercourse.
If a reuse system is already operating and the water smells bad, pools or harms plants, stop using it and seek qualified local advice.
